reason: I want to follow how blood is filtered into urine, starting with the kidney's filtering unit.
expectation: I expect the nephron to filter some fluid and dissolved substances from the blood, though I'm unsure how much detail the result will show.

alternatives.reason: Connecting the ureters would advance the other goal, but I want to follow filtration first.

effect: The filter separates blood cells and most proteins from fluid and small dissolved substances, so the next question is what the tubule recovers.
reaction: The distinction makes the filtration step clear.
reason: I want to follow the filtered fluid through recovery, and the transporters seem suited to returning useful substances.
expectation: I expect some useful dissolved substances to move from the tubule back toward the blood, though the result may specify which ones.

alternatives.reason: The ureters would advance the urinary-organ connection, but I want to finish following filtration first.

effect: The tubule recovers glucose and other useful substances, so I want to follow what happens to the water next.
reaction: Recovering nearly all filtered glucose makes the kidney's selective role clearer.
reason: The water-permeable tubule should show how water is recovered before urine leaves.
expectation: I expect some water to move from the tubule back toward the blood, leaving a more concentrated fluid.

effect: Water returns to the blood while wastes remain in the tubule, so the remaining fluid can now be followed into urinary drainage.
reaction: The contrast between recovered water and remaining wastes is clear.
reason: I want to finish following the filtered sample to urine before connecting the organs.
expectation: I expect the remaining fluid to enter the urinary drainage route as urine.

effect: The remaining fluid has entered the ureter and bladder as urine, completing the filtration goal; I can now connect the urinary organs.
reaction: Following the sample from filtration to the bladder made the route clear.
reason: The ureters connect the kidneys to the bladder, so I will attach them first.
expectation: I expect the ureters to be fitted to the kidney pair, leaving the bladder to connect.

alternatives.reason: The bladder also needs fitting, but the ureters follow the urine's route from the kidneys.

effect: The ureters are fitted to the kidneys, leaving the bladder to complete the drainage route.
reaction: The fitting is straightforward, though it adds little beyond the route already shown.
reason: Attaching the bladder is the only available combination and advances the urinary-organ goal.
expectation: I expect the bladder to be fitted to the kidney and ureter assembly.

effect: The bladder is fitted, completing the urinary drainage assembly; the remaining combination connects it to the body.
reaction: The route is clear, though the explanation repeats the earlier urine result.
reason: Connecting the urinary organs to the body is the only available combination and advances the remaining goal.
expectation: I expect the kidneys and urinary drainage organs to become part of the connected body.

effect: The urinary organs are now connected to circulation, completing the chapter's second goal.
reaction: The final picture ties the filtering process to the wider body clearly.

mostWorthwhile.text: Following the filtered sample through nutrient and water recovery was most worthwhile: it showed that kidneys reclaim useful materials as well as remove waste.

leastWorthwhile.text: Fitting the ureters and bladder felt repetitive after the urine had already been shown traveling to the bladder.

surprise.text: Learning that healthy kidneys normally recover almost all filtered glucose made their selective role clearer.

arbitrary.text: No action felt purposeless, though the organ fittings repeated a route already shown and offered little new information.

continue.text: I would be interested in another chapter if it developed a similarly clear connection between body systems, though repeated assembly steps would make me less eager.
